checklist.fact: The City of Federal Way (WA) is the issuer, seeking proposals from experienced, qualified Vendors that can provide ERP software and services meeting all of the City's functional and technical requirements.
The City intends to purchase an integrated ERP solution and to implement it as a replacement ERP, using a phased approach or one recommended by the selected Vendor and approved by the City.
The City will also accept responses from vendors offering best-of-breed Human Capital Management solutions, which must be able to integrate with the selected ERP system.
Proposals are due September 17, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, and late submissions will not be considered.
Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, with the RFP issued August 16, 2024.
The estimated timeline has implementation running from March 2025 to January 2027, after finalist selection in October 2024, demos in December 2024, and due diligence in January 2025.

Proposals are scored on Software (30), Technology (15), Vendor (15), Cost Value (15) and Implementation (25), and the Implementation criterion requires Go Live for all modules in scope by January 1, 2027.
Pricing must be comprehensive (including all taxes and discounts), valid for 180 days, and cover software, implementation services, and license/maintenance for Years 1-10.
Proposals must be emailed as one PDF of no more than 100 pages (excluding sample contracts) plus the Requirements document in MS Word format.
The pricing basis is 130 named users and 85 concurrent users for Financials, and 400 FTEs and 744 W2s for Human Capital Management.

The detailed modules and functionality are defined in a separate Requirements Word document that is not included in this PDF; vendors must rate each item, and missing many Required features may lead to elimination.

The new ERP replaces Eden (financials, HR, time and attendance, payroll), Quadrant cashiering and Excel-based budget and ACFR, and must integrate with retained systems such as NeoGov, Power Time, Amanda and RecTrac.

component_records.title: Engagement governance, compliance and contract obligations
component_records.description: A single governance workstream owns everything contractual so nothing is left to a technical appendix. It delivers the signed acknowledgment of the RFP terms and exhibits, the exceptions log, the certification of insurance with underwriter's endorsement and Washington-admitted surety before any work starts, and the data-ownership and public-disclosure position confirming all data, materials and documentation prepared for the City belong to the City and that no entire submittal is marked proprietary. It also runs the steering committee, status reporting, risk and issue logs, and change control across the March 2025–January 2027 schedule, and confirms the vendor bears its own bid costs.

component_records.title: Phased implementation programme and project plan
component_records.description: We deliver a phased implementation plan — discovery and fit-gap, then configuration, conversion, integration and reporting, then testing, training and cutover — with a sample project plan showing phases, tasks and timeline, and a resource matrix giving City and Vendor roles, responsibilities and average hours per month. The plan is sequenced against the City's hard deadline so all modules in scope reach Go Live by January 1, 2027, with contingency held before the deadline rather than after it. Where the City prefers an alternative sequencing, we present it for City approval as the RFP allows.

component_records.title: Financials module configuration
component_records.description: Configuration of the required Financial modules — General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets and Enterprise Cashiering — against the City's Requirements document, line by line, with a rating and a comment for every item. Configuration follows the vendor's standard best practices rather than replicating current City processes, in line with the City's stated process-improvement driver, and each deviation is documented as a fit-gap decision. Every functional and technical requirement in the Requirements document is answered, so the City can verify coverage before award.

component_records.title: Human Capital Management, including best-of-breed integration
component_records.description: Delivery of Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll, sized to 400 FTEs and 744 W2s, with payroll and time-collection interfaces to the Financials modules so labour costs post to the general ledger without re-keying. Where the City selects a best-of-breed HCM product rather than the ERP vendor's own, we deliver the integration layer — file and API-based interfaces, error handling and reconciliation reporting — and demonstrate that the HCM solution integrates with the selected ERP. The same configuration and requirements-response discipline applies to HCM as to Financials.

component_records.title: Data conversion, integration and report development
component_records.description: A conversion workstream covering extraction, cleansing, mapping, mock loads and reconciliation for master data and balances from the City's existing ERP environment, with City sign-off on each converted dataset before cutover. Integration tooling connects the ERP to the City's other systems, and a report development track replaces current custom reports and delivers the City's operational and management reporting using standard tools. Both are priced as implementation services and included in the go-live scope.

component_records.title: Testing, training and change management
component_records.description: A structured test programme — unit, integration, conference-room pilot, user acceptance and parallel payroll — with documented entry and exit criteria tied to the January 1, 2027 Go Live. Training is role-based for finance, purchasing, HR and payroll staff and for approvers and casual users, delivered through train-the-trainer and quick-reference materials, and supported by a change management plan covering stakeholder communication, readiness assessment and post-go-live adoption support. Methodologies for testing, training and change management are documented in the implementation overview.

component_records.title: Deployment architecture: SaaS and on-premises options
component_records.description: Two fully specified deployment options, each with its own architecture, data centre locations and redundancy design, hardware specifications where on-premises, mobile and remote access approach, integration tools and software update schedule. The security model is documented for each option, covering SSO/SAML, multi-factor authentication and breach notification, response and cost. Both options are priced separately so the City can compare them on equal terms.

component_records.title: Pricing on Exhibit A, sized to the City's user counts
component_records.description: Pricing is completed on the Exhibit A Pricing Summary as Section 3 of the response, covering software and implementation services for all Required modules, with a separate sheet for each deployment option. It is built on 130 named and 85 concurrent Financials users and 400 FTEs and 744 W2s for HCM, includes all taxes and available discounts, and carries ten years of license/maintenance. The price is held valid for 180 days from the response date, and implementation pricing covers deployment, conversion, configuration, reporting, testing and training through go live.

component_records.title: Demonstrations, references and bidder qualification
component_records.description: We prepare and deliver the on-site functional and technical demonstration strictly to the Demo Script issued with the finalist invitation, with presenters briefed to discuss best practices and how the system adapts to user preferences. The bid package carries three current and two prior customer references on the Exhibit B forms, weighted toward Washington State public-sector clients of comparable size and scope, plus the five-year disclosure of any terminated contract or customer legal action. This component also covers the vendor's own bid costs and the written question process ahead of the August 28, 2024 deadline.

items.text: The RFP is issued by the City of Federal Way, Washington, which incorporated in February 1990 and changed from a council-manager to a mayor-council form of government in November 2010.

The City is a residential and commercial municipality with an estimated 22,485 people employed within its city limits, and its comprehensive plan calls for a vibrant City Center with mixed-use development and public transportation access.

The City is replacing an existing ERP environment, and the RFP's Scope section presents tables describing that current environment and which solutions are in scope, but those tables are not reproduced in the RFP text.
The City's stated business driver is process improvement through new systems, and it intends to adopt the best practices offered by the selected Vendor rather than replicate current processes.
The City's sizing baseline is 130 named and 85 concurrent Financials users, and 400 FTEs and 744 W2s for Human Capital Management.
The City is open to best-of-breed Human Capital Management proposals from Vendors that are not ERP providers, provided the HCM solution can integrate with the selected ERP system.
The City wants to procure an integrated ERP software solution plus implementation services covering all modules and functionality defined in the separate Requirements document.

The required Financial modules are General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets and Enterprise Cashiering, and the required Human Capital Management modules are Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll.
The City expects a phased implementation approach, or another approach recommended by the selected Vendor and approved by the City.
Implementation is scheduled to run from March 2025 through January 2027, with all modules in scope required to Go Live by January 1, 2027.

Implementation services must cover software deployment, data conversion, system configuration, report development, testing and training, and pricing must include license/maintenance costs for Years 1 through 10.

The Requirements document is provided as a separate Word document that becomes Section 2 of the proposal, and the current-environment and in-scope solution tables referenced in the Scope section are not included in the RFP text, so bidders must obtain them.
The City requires insurance certification and an underwriter's endorsement before any work begins, with a surety admitted in Washington State.

Requirements document not in hand, so scope and price rest on an unseen document. The ERP Requirements document is a separate Word file that becomes Section 2 of the proposal and defines the full functional and technical scope, but it is not part of the RFP text. The bid is priced and staffed against an assumed scope; if the document is larger or deeper than assumed, the fixed implementation price and the January 1, 2027 date both move. The scope of the entire engagement is defined by a document the bidder does not yet hold, and the RFP makes blank requirement responses grounds for rejection.

Current-environment and in-scope solution tables missing, so conversion is scoped blind. The Scope section refers to tables describing the City's existing ERP environment and which solutions are in scope, but those tables are not reproduced in the RFP. The proposed solution assumes a single incumbent ERP replaced in full; if the City actually runs several systems, or keeps some in place, data conversion, integration and cutover effort grow well beyond the priced scope. Conversion is a large, hard-to-absorb cost line and the source landscape is unknown; the solution's single-source assumption is stated as an inference, not a fact.

Fixed January 1, 2027 go-live across all modules with no schedule float. Every module in scope — eight Financials modules plus HR, Time and Attendance and Payroll — must be live by January 1, 2027, inside a March 2025 to January 2027 window, and the Implementation criterion is scored on that date. A single late dependency, such as a delayed City decision, a failed parallel payroll or a conversion rework, consumes the contingency and pushes the date. Missing it costs the City its fiscal-year start and exposes the bidder to contractual remedies. The date is hard, scored and covers a broad module set including payroll parallel runs; the solution holds contingency before the deadline but the RFP leaves no room to move it.

Submission mechanics and page-limit counting left ambiguous. The RFP points to an email address for receipt but also refers to a location indicated above and to a published list of submitters, and it is unclear whether the 100-page limit covers the PDF only or the PDF plus the Word Requirements document. A misjudged page count or a delivery method the City does not accept could disqualify an otherwise strong proposal, and late submissions are not considered. Disqualification is severe, but the RFP's Sections 5 and 9 restate email submission and the PDF limit clearly enough that the risk turns on a clarification the City can give.

City resource commitments assumed but not confirmed. The plan depends on City subject-matter experts giving the monthly hours shown in the sample project plan for fit-gap, configuration decisions, testing and sign-off. If those people are not available at the assumed level, discovery and testing slip and the bidder absorbs the rework or the date moves. The RFP does not state what City staffing the City will commit. Two full deployment options double the architecture and pricing effort. The proposal must document hosted, on-premises and SaaS architecture, data centre locations, redundancy, hardware specifications and a security model for each, and price each option on its own sheet. Producing two complete, defensible designs and price books within the 100-page limit and the response window stretches the bid team and risks a thin, low-scoring technology section. Insurance limits and additional-insured terms unknown before contract. The City requires a certificate of insurance with an underwriter's endorsement and additional insured verbiage, and a surety admitted in Washington, before any work begins, but the RFP does not state coverage types, limits or who must be named. The obligation is a precondition to starting work, and the solution's assumption of customary municipal limits is unconfirmed.

Exhibit A template not in hand, so pricing structure is assumed. Pricing must be submitted on the Exhibit A Pricing Summary as Section 3, with a separate sheet per deployment option and ten years of license and maintenance, but the template itself is not in the RFP text. If the template's rows or formulas do not accommodate the bidder's structure, the pricing section must be rebuilt late in the response window, and a mis-mapped price is easy to score badly on Cost Value. Cost Value carries 15 points and the template's structure is unknown; the solution's assumption that one workbook accepts a sheet per option is unverified.

Best-of-breed HCM integration priced on an unknown ERP pairing. The City will accept an HCM product from a vendor that is not an ERP provider provided it integrates with the selected ERP, and the solution offers to build that integration layer. If the City pairs the bidder's HCM with a third-party ERP, the interface work, error handling and reconciliation are scoped against an API the bidder does not control, and the effort can exceed the priced integration. The RFP explicitly opens the door to mixed-vendor stacks, and the solution commits to delivering the integration layer without knowing the counterpart system.

Page 5 unreadable, so part of the instructions may be missed. Page 5 of the RFP is dominated by an image that could not be read, covering 42 percent of the page. If that page carries submission instructions, a required form or a scoring detail, the proposal could omit a mandatory element or be judged non-responsive. The unreadable block is large and sits in the early instruction pages, but the rest of the RFP restates the submission rules in Sections 5 and 9.

Requirement responses constrained to 100 words with no cross-references. Every line item in the Requirements document must be rated on the 4/3/2/0/F scale with a comment of no more than 100 words, no hyperlinks and no references to other line items, and a rating of 2 must carry a modification cost while a rating of 3 must name the third-party product. With a large requirement set this is a substantial writing and quality-control effort, and a blank or generic answer can cause rejection. The RFP treats blank responses as grounds for rejection and forbids the shortcuts (cross-references, 'standard functionality') that would make the volume manageable.

Proprietary marking and public disclosure conflict with normal bid protection. All submitted materials become the City's property and are subject to public disclosure, no vendor may mark its entire submittal proprietary, and the City alone decides what is proprietary. Pricing detail, security design and integration architecture therefore become public, which the bidder may not expect and which can expose commercially sensitive information to competitors. The RFP states the position plainly and the solution accepts it, so the exposure is certain but the commercial impact is limited to disclosure of bid content.
